summary:
DRIFT (Dynamic Rapid Infrared Frame-Tracking & Blink Comparator) is an advanced web application developed to bridge the gap between archival NASA sky surveys and rapid astronomical discovery. Built using a React frontend and a Python FastAPI backend, DRIFT interfaces directly with NASA's public SkyView and Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) APIs to ingest multi-epoch infrared imagery from premier missions like WISE and 2MASS.

To address the challenge of shifting through massive repositories of celestial data, DRIFT features a high-precision optical blink comparator equipped with variable-frequency frame alternation, split-screen wipe sliders, difference imaging, and sub-pixel astrometric alignment tools. These features allow users to instantly isolate moving objects, proper-motion stars, and transient infrared phenomena that would otherwise remain hidden in static frames.

This project is important because it democratizes access to complex space science data, empowering researchers, students, and citizen scientists to perform efficient data-driven visual analysis, preliminary planetary defence screening, and multi-wavelength astronomical research
details:
The universe is in constant motion, yet the most critical dynamic events—near-Earth asteroids, high-proper-motion brown dwarfs, and transient infrared phenomena—often hide in plain sight within vast petabytes of archival sky surveys. DRIFT bridges the gap between raw NASA infrared survey archives and rapid human-in-the-loop anomaly detection. Engineered as a modern, browser-based astrometric blink comparator, DRIFT empowers researchers, citizen scientists, and students to retrieve, align, and visually interrogate multi-epoch, multi-wavelength NASA infrared imagery in real time—transforming static archival data into actionable astronomical discoveries.

Technical Architecture & Core Capabilities

  • Direct NASA Survey Archive Integration: DRIFT interfaces directly with NASA’s public SkyView Virtual Observatory and Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) APIs to ingest uncalibrated and unaltered FITS/JPEG imagery across premier infrared missions, including the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) (3.4µm, 4.6µm, 12µm, and 22µm bands) and the Two Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS) (J, H, and K near-infrared bands). Users can query targets by common astronomical nomenclature or precise Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates, with full access to native mission metadata and original source files.
    • Variable-Frequency Blink Alternation: Rapidly cycles between Epoch/Band A and Epoch/Band B at user-defined intervals (0.1s to 3.0s), leveraging human visual motion sensitivity to isolate moving bodies and variable flux sources.
    • Interactive Split-Screen Wipe & Difference Blending: Allows continuous spatial comparison via a real-time split-screen divider, alongside difference-imaging and false-color overlay modes that suppress static background starfields while amplifying thermal dust structures and transient anomalies.
  • Sub-Pixel Astrometric Alignment & Radiometric Scaling: To account for spacecraft roll-angle variations and multi-mission astrometric offsets, DRIFT incorporates sub-pixel X/Y translation controls and synchronized pan-and-zoom locking. Researchers can dynamically toggle between linear, logarithmic (log), and square-root (sqrt) pixel intensity stretches to resolve faint interstellar nebulosity alongside high-luminosity stellar cores.
  • Transient Logging & Hybrid Local/Cloud Processing: DRIFT includes an integrated annotation suite that enables users to tag candidate anomalies directly on the celestial canvas, automatically recording celestial/pixel coordinates and generating exportable session logs for follow-up observation. Built on a decoupled React/TypeScript frontend with a dual-mode architecture, DRIFT operates seamlessly in Direct NASA Live Mode for zero-latency cloud access while supporting a Local Python FastAPI Backend for custom automated image-processing pipelines.

Scientific Impact & Alignment with NASA Objectives

By lowering the computational barrier to multi-band infrared analysis, DRIFT democratizes access to NASA’s open-science data repositories. Whether used for preliminary planetary defense screening, comparative stellar evolution studies, or STEM education, DRIFT accelerates the path from archival observation to scientific discovery.


Tools, Technologies & Data Resources Used

1. NASA Data Archives & Astronomical APIs

  • NASA SkyView Virtual Observatory (GSFC HEASARC): Used for real-time retrieval and rendering of multi-wavelength sky cutouts via target names or J2000 RA/Dec coordinates.
  • NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA): Utilized as the primary repository for calibrated infrared science products and archival mission metadata.
  • WISE / NEOWISE (Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer): Ingested mid-infrared survey imagery across four bands (W1: 3.4 µm, W2: 4.6 µm, W3: 12 µm, W4: 22 µm) to detect thermal dust, brown dwarfs, and moving objects.
  • 2MASS (Two Micron All Sky Survey): Ingested near-infrared survey imagery across three channels (J: 1.235 µm, H: 1.662 µm, Ks: 2.159 µm) to peer through dense interstellar dust clouds.
  • NASA FITS Format & World Coordinate System (WCS): Used for raw astronomical pixel analysis, header inspection, and celestial coordinate mapping (supported via SIMBAD and NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database (NED) name resolution).

2. Frontend Coding & UI Frameworks

  • React & TypeScript: Core libraries used to build the interactive browser-based blink comparator dashboard and user interface.
  • Vite: Frontend build tool and development server for fast application bundling.
  • Tailwind CSS & Lucide Icons: Used for responsive dark-mode observatory styling and clean scientific iconography.
  • TanStack Start: Used for client-side routing and data fetching architecture.

3. Backend, Scientific Analysis & Deployment

  • Python: Primary backend programming language for scientific data handling.
  • FastAPI: High-performance Python API framework used for backend astronomical processing endpoints.
  • Astropy: Core astronomy library used for parsing FITS files, handling WCS transformations, and performing astrometric alignment calculations.
  • GitHub: Used for source code version control and repository hosting.
  • Vercel: Used for continuous deployment and global public hosting of the live web application.

4. AI Assistants, Research & Presentation Tools

  • Lovable: Used for rapid full-stack web prototyping and UI component scaffolding.
  • Google Gemini, Claude, & ChatGPT: Used as AI development co-pilots for debugging API integrations, refining astrometric math logic, and structuring technical documentation.
  • Perplexity: Used for rapid astrophysics literature lookups, mission band specifications, and technical verification.
  • Gamma: Used to design and structure the 7-slide visual presentation deck for the project demonstration.

AI Usage Disclosure: AI tools (Google Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Lovable, and Gamma) were used to assist with frontend prototyping, debugging API workflows, astrophysical research, and structuring presentation materials. All astronomical imagery and scientific data are sourced directly from official NASA open archives.
